title: Product & Recipe Filters
blurb: A reusable, live client-side filtering app built for food-service brands.

hero.hint: A screenshot of the filters in action
hero.alt: Screenshot of an online store displaying pasta products, including Marzetti frozen elbow macaroni, farfalle, penne rigati, cavatappi, and elbow macaroni, with filters on the left side.

case.lede: A reusable, live client-side filtering app built for food-service brands.
context: Product and recipe catalogs are only useful if people can find what they're looking for. For a set of food-service clients, the existing approach either relied on server-side filtering — every filter selection triggered a full page reload, making the experience slow and frustrating — or apps with limited functionality, like only a single filtering option. The goal was live, client-side filtering: accurate, usable, and fast, without the page ever refreshing.
case.roleDetail: Sole developer across all implementations. Each client had its own visual design handled by a designer; the filtering logic, data architecture, and front-end build were entirely my own.

decisions.title: Building for reuse
decisions.body: Although the initial build was a one-off, it was soon clear that a reusable version would be valuable as the same problem kept presenting itself with new projects. The final app was architected as a base that could be adapted across sites with different product catalogs and visual designs. The filtering logic was kept separate from the presentation layer so each client's design could be applied without touching the core functionality.

decisions.title: From GraphQL to a server-side JS object
decisions.body: The original version pulled product data from Craft CMS via its GraphQL API, which worked well. When the app was adapted for WordPress, WPGraphQL was the natural equivalent. However, it didn't perform well enough under real conditions. The solution was to shift data loading to a server-side built JavaScript object, constructed at render time and cached with typical WordPress caching strategies. This kept the client-side experience fast while avoiding the overhead of a runtime API call.

decisions.title: Dynamic filter generation
decisions.body: When the app loads, all product data is read in and the filtering menu is generated dynamically by reading each product's tags. New filter options appear automatically as the product catalog changes with no manual menu maintenance required.

decisions.title: The filtering logic
decisions.body: The core of the app is a computed function that handles a nuanced filtering pattern: within a group, selected filters are OR (show me items matching any of these), but between groups they are AND (show me items matching at least one from each group). This mirrors how people actually think about filtering: ‘show me chicken or beef dishes, but only the ones that are also gluten-free.’

decisions.title: URL parameter sync
decisions.body: Filter state and pagination are reflected in the URL as query parameters, which unlocks a few things that users take for granted but implementations often skip: the browser back and forward buttons work as expected, filtered views can be bookmarked or shared as direct links, and pre-filtered URLs can be constructed and linked to from other pages. It's a small detail that makes the app feel native to the web rather than bolted onto it.

decisions.title: Search with Fuse.js
decisions.body: Basic string searching is handled by Fuse.js, giving users a way to search across the catalog without a server round-trip. Fuse operates against the already-loaded data, keeping the experience consistent with the live filtering approach.

outcome: The app is currently live on several client sites across different brands and product catalogs, handling both product and recipe filtering. The shift from WPGraphQL to a server-side JS object resolved the performance issues and became the standard data approach for all subsequent WordPress implementations.
reflections: In hindsight, the volume of WordPress implementations makes a strong case for packaging this as a proper plugin with an admin interface for filter configuration, rather than manual setup. It's the natural next step for something that's become a recurring solution.

title: All Spreads Daymaker
blurb: A recipe discovery app for a food-service brand that arranges recipes on a programmatically generated SVG clock, organized by daypart.

hero.hint: A screenshot of the Daymaker app
hero.alt: Smucker’s Day Maker tool lets users spin a wheel of meal ideas with photos of dishes. On the right, a box offers options to explore recipes: Breakfasts, Entrees, or Snacks & Sweets, with a red checkered border below.

case.lede: To facilitate recipe discovery using the client's products, the Daymaker app arranges recipes in a circular manner, resembling a clock.
context: Daypart filtering is a common need in food-service recipe discovery -- a chef or menu planner looking to fill a breakfast gap thinks differently than one planning dinner. The client wanted a recipe discovery experience that made dayparts the organizing principle, presented in a way that felt distinctive and engaging rather than a standard filtered list.

The design called for a clock UI: recipes arranged in a circle, color-coded by daypart, with a fork and knife pointer. The challenge was that the number of recipes per daypart is variable -- pulled live from a CMS API -- meaning the size of each slice, and the position of every element on the clock, had to be calculated programmatically after the data loaded.
case.roleDetail: Sole developer on the app. A separate developer built and maintained the Pimcore REST API; a designer provided complete designs for both the desktop clock and mobile pie chart views. The SVG generation, trigonometric calculations, animation, and Vue architecture were entirely my own work.

decisions.title: Generating the clock as SVG
decisions.body: The entire clock is built programmatically in Vue -- there is no static SVG base. Recipes, daypart slices, markers, labels, and color coding are all computed and rendered from the API data. Color coding is data-driven from the CMS, making it easy to update without touching the front end.

decisions.title: The trig problem
decisions.body: Because the number of recipes per daypart varies, the angular size of each slice varies too. Placing recipe markers and daypart labels at the correct positions on the circle required trigonometric calculations after each data load. The calculations needed to handle centering each daypart's recipes within its slice, accumulating angles correctly across dayparts, and converting between degrees and radians for SVG coordinate math.

decisions.title: Trigonometry for variable item placement
decisions.body: AI assistance was instrumental in working out the correct trigonometric functions for variable item placement -- a problem that is easy to get subtly wrong and hard to debug visually.

decisions.title: Animation
decisions.body: GreenSock (GSAP) handles the fork and knife pointer animation, adding a tactile, satisfying quality to interacting with the clock that a CSS transition alone wouldn't achieve.

decisions.title: Mobile adaptation
decisions.body: The desktop clock gives way to a simpler pie chart on mobile, letting users tap a daypart to select it. The switch was a practical design decision -- the full clock UI doesn't translate well to touch targets and narrow viewports, but the core daypart-first navigation concept carries over cleanly.

outcome: The app successfully surfaces recipes organized by daypart in a distinctive, visually engaging format. The variable slice calculation handles real-world data gracefully, and the mobile pie chart provides a usable fallback without sacrificing the daypart-first concept.

title: Web Design for Design Majors
blurb: Course materials for a course on web design and development.

hero.hint: A sampling of styletiles from the course
hero.alt: A collage of various website mockups displaying different fonts, colors, layouts, and graphic elements, showcasing diverse web design styles and branding approaches.

case.lede: Course materials for a course on web design and development.
context: Graphic design and illustration students need to understand how the web works and how to design for it. However, most arrive with no development experience and mixed interest in ever writing code. The challenge wasn't just teaching web design and development concepts; it was teaching them in a way that respected both the students who would go deep and the ones who just needed a basic understanding of development.
case.roleDetail: Sole instructor for one section of the course, which ran alongside a colleague's parallel section. Responsible for all instruction, course structure, and materials within the university's course description. Some projects were inherited from previous instructors; the course site, lectures, and overall approach were my own.

decisions.title: Isolated exercises over a single running project
decisions.body: Coding concepts were introduced through small, self-contained CodePen exercises and pre-built boilerplates rather than one accumulating project. This lowered the stakes for students who struggled and kept the focus on the concept at hand rather than debugging something they built three weeks ago.

decisions.title: Live demonstration as preview, not instruction
decisions.body: Coding lectures were designed to show how things work in context, not to be followed along in real time. Students watched, asked questions, then applied concepts in the exercises. This reduced the chaos of live coding sessions where half the class falls behind on a semicolon.

decisions.title: The course site as a resource
decisions.body: Built with VuePress, the site housed all course materials and was developed live during in-class demos, giving students a real example to reference throughout the semester.

outcome: All students came away with a working understanding of designing for the web. The coding component was more variable — predictably so, as it tracked closely with individual student interest. That's an honest outcome for a design-first audience where web development is a supporting skill, not the primary focus.
reflections: The mixed coding results point to an inherent tension in the course: it serves students who want to build things and students who just need to understand the medium, and those are genuinely different courses. A future version might split the track earlier or lean harder into the design-for-web angle and treat coding as optional depth rather than a shared requirement.

title: Smucker's Fun
blurb: A lightweight, web app for restaurant diners waiting on breakfast.

hero.hint: A screenshot of the Fun app
hero.alt: A white wooden background with berries at the top. Text reads, “Make your wait less wait-y.” Below are two green buttons labeled “Conversation Starters” and “Trivia,” with a red checkered tablecloth at the bottom.

case.lede: A lightweight, web app for restaurant diners waiting on breakfast.
context: Smucker's single-serve spread caddies sit on restaurant tables, and the wait for breakfast is dead time. The goal was to give diners something to do with that time -- something light, social, and on-brand. A QR code on the caddy leads to a simple web app with two modes: conversation starters and fill-in-the-blank trivia across several categories.

The user arrives with zero context -- they scanned a code on a condiment caddy and have no idea what they're about to see. The app needed to be immediately legible without any onboarding or explanation.
case.roleDetail: Sole developer. Had brief early input into the experience before design kicked off; the designer provided complete designs and the build was entirely my own.

decisions.title: Letting the UI speak for itself
decisions.body: With no onboarding and a user who may have never heard of the app, the interface had to be self-explanatory on first glance. No tutorial, no welcome screen, no instructions -- just an experience that makes its own purpose clear immediately. That constraint shaped every decision about layout, hierarchy, and interaction.

decisions.title: Performance as a baseline
decisions.body: Restaurant wifi is unpredictable and the app needed to load fast on a cold visit from a QR code scan. Performance was a priority from the start -- Nuxt's server-side rendering and a lean stack with no heavy dependencies kept the initial load light.

decisions.title: CSS Transforms for interaction
decisions.body: Animation and transitions are handled with CSS Transforms rather than a JavaScript animation library, keeping the bundle lean while still giving the interactions a polished, tactile feel appropriate for a casual, fun experience.

decisions.title: Content in the store
decisions.body: Trivia content across all categories lives in the Pinia store -- a deliberate simplicity for a one-time content load with no requirement for ongoing updates. No CMS overhead, no API calls, just fast access to everything the app needs on load.

outcome: The app is live and accessible via QR code on Smucker's branded table caddies in participating restaurants. The self-explanatory UI successfully handles a zero-context entry point, dropping users straight into the experience without instruction.

title: Jif That Dish
blurb: A Vue app that randomly surfaces menu applications for Jif Peanut Butter recipes, with filtering and sequential browsing

hero.hint: A screenshot of the Wheel app
hero.alt: A colorful Jif peanut butter-themed game wheel with sections for different dip ideas, surrounded by images of food, and text suggesting ways to serve Jif, flavor hacks, and a PB Hummus Dip recipe.

case.lede: A Vue app that randomly surfaces menu applications for Jif Peanut Butter recipes, with filtering and sequential browsing
context: Food-service clients need to sell chefs and menu planners on how a product fits into their menu. For Jif Peanut Butter, the goal was a fun, engaging way to surface recipe applications randomly -- giving a user a reason to keep spinning and discovering rather than browsing a static list. Filtering and sequential browsing round out the experience for users who want more control.
case.roleDetail: Sole front-end developer. A separate developer built and maintained the same Pimcore REST API used across the Marlin food-service project family. Designer provided complete designs.

decisions.title: Rethinking the wheel
decisions.body: The original concept called for a Wheel of Fortune style spinning wheel -- slots, labels, the works. In a problem-solving meeting, I flagged that the trigonometric complexity of a variable-slot wheel would be significant, and proposed an alternative: a Price is Right style wheel, where a single continuous drum spins and lands on a result. Simpler to implement, just as satisfying to interact with, and the client agreed. It was a practical trade-off that kept the project on track without sacrificing the core mechanic.

decisions.title: Animation with GSAP
decisions.body: GreenSock handles the wheel spin animation. The goal was a spin that feels physical -- building momentum, then decelerating naturally to a stop. GSAP gave fine control over easing and duration, though getting the speed curves to feel truly realistic proved harder than expected.

decisions.title: Filtering and sequential browsing
decisions.body: Beyond the random spin, users can filter by category and walk through applications one at a time. This gave more deliberate users a way to explore the full catalog without relying on chance.

outcome: The app successfully delivers a fun, randomized recipe discovery experience for food-service audiences, with enough structure for users who want to browse more intentionally.
reflections: The animation was the most challenging part and the part I'm least satisfied with. Making a spinning wheel feel physically convincing requires fine-tuned speed curves that are harder to dial in than they look -- the spin works, but it lacks the weight and deceleration of something truly realistic. It was a valuable lesson in how much craft goes into motion that feels natural, and something I'd approach differently with more time or a second pass.
Additionally, the similar All Spreads Daymaker app that I later built showed that the Wheel of Fortune style wheel would have been possible and probably moreeffective.

title: Alchemedia Project Website
blurb: An advertising agency website built with Nuxt.js and Prismic

hero.hint: A screenshot of the Alchemedia project website
hero.alt: A blue-tinted office background with bold black text saying “Hey There.” Smaller white text below reads, “If food is what you do (even part of what you do) you’ve landed in the right spot.”.

case.lede: An advertising agency website built with Nuxt.js and Prismic
context: The Alchemedia Project needed a marketing site covering agency messaging, team information, and case studies. As an internal project, it presented a low-risk opportunity to try a headless CMS approach for the first time -- taking on the experimentation risk ourselves rather than on a client's time and budget.
case.roleDetail: Lead developer on the project, with junior developers assisting. Ryan Baker handled all design work. Responsible for the overall technical approach, Prismic integration, and front-end build.

decisions.title: Choosing headless as a learning opportunity
decisions.body: Internal projects are a good time to experiment with new ways of working -- the risk is yours to take rather than a client's. Prismic was a deliberate choice to get hands-on experience with a headless CMS in a real production context. The content modeling and API-driven approach were new territory, and working through it on an internal project meant the learning curve didn't come at anyone else's expense.

decisions.title: The manual data fetching problem
decisions.body: One of the less glamorous realities of working with Prismic at the time was the amount of manual data fetching required -- every content type needed its own fetch logic, which added up to a lot of repetitive code. It was a real friction point, and one that modern AI tooling would make trivial today. It didn't block the project, but it shaped an appreciation for the value of good SDK abstractions.

decisions.title: CSS techniques pushed by the design
decisions.body: Ryan's designs called for visual techniques that were outside my existing toolkit at the time: text-strokes, rotated type, SVG masks, and image masks. Implementing them required digging into CSS capabilities I didn't know existed. That kind of designer-led technical stretch is one of the better ways to expand what you know -- the design sets the bar and you figure out how to meet it.

outcome: The site launched successfully and served The Alchemedia Project until the agency was absorbed into another company. It's no longer live, but it achieved its goals as both a functioning agency website and a genuine learning exercise -- establishing a foundation for headless CMS work that carried into future projects.

title: Accessibility Dev Training
blurb: A living accessibility reference and training document written for a team of six developers -- covering foundational concepts, common problem areas, and practical solutions to raise the baseline across new work.

hero.hint: A screenshot of the Accessibility Dev Training document
hero.alt: A webpage section titled “Scope” explains web accessibility, quoting Heydon Pickering, and discusses making sites usable for all. A yellow-highlighted note says, “If a website isn’t accessible, it isn’t usable.”.

case.lede: A living accessibility reference and training document written for a team of six developers -- covering foundational concepts, common problem areas, and practical solutions to raise the baseline across new work.
context: Web accessibility is easy to deprioritize and hard to retrofit. As part of a company-driven effort to raise the team's knowledge, I researched and wrote a training document aimed at developers who understood the concept of accessibility but needed practical guidance on implementation -- what it actually means to make a project accessible, where the hard problems are, and how to approach testing.
case.roleDetail: Lead researcher and author. The training was a collaborative research effort across the team; I synthesized the findings into a single cohesive document and led any subsequent training sessions.

decisions.title: Structuring for reference, not just reading
decisions.body: As a living document rather than a one-time presentation, the training needed to work as something developers would return to -- not just read once and forget. That shaped how it was organized: high-level concepts up front, with deeper dives into specific problem areas that developers could jump to as needed.

decisions.title: Focusing on the hard problems
decisions.body: Rather than cataloging every WCAG success criterion, the training zeroed in on the areas that cause the most trouble in practice: multimedia accessibility, keyboard navigation patterns -- including the notoriously tricky problem of accessible dropdown navigation -- and testing strategies. These are the areas where good intentions most often fall short, and where concrete guidance has the most impact.

decisions.title: Testing strategies as a practical anchor
decisions.body: Accessibility testing is often overlooked until it's too late. Including testing strategies -- not just implementation guidance -- gave developers a way to verify their work rather than assume it was correct.

outcome: The document became a living reference for a team of six developers. Following the training, accessible code became a baseline expectation for new work -- with the reasonable caveat that stakeholder priorities or budget constraints could affect specific features. That's an honest outcome: it shifted the default without pretending those realities don't exist.
reflections: Not all stakeholders understand the nuts and bolts of accessibility, but the training helped raise awareness of it as a concept and why it matters -- which is its own kind of progress. Accessibility techniques also take practice, and taking the time to go deep on the subject was worth the effort even when individual projects fall short. Getting it right consistently is a long game.

title: Fluid Type Tester
blurb: A personal tool for testing fluid and static type scales in the browser

hero.hint: Screenshot of the Fluid Type Tester tool
hero.alt: A web tool called “Fluid Type Tester” shows adjustable sliders for font sizes and a preview area with the opening text from “Alice in Wonderland” under the heading “Down the Rabbit-Hole.”.

case.lede: A personal tool for testing fluid and static type scales in the browser
context: Fluid typography uses CSS clamp to allow font sizes to scale smoothly with the viewport -- rather than jumping between fixed sizes at breakpoints, type grows and shrinks continuously between a defined minimum and maximum. It's a powerful technique, but visualizing how a fluid type scale actually behaves across viewport widths requires either resizing your browser constantly or guessing.

A few tools existed for this, but none had the combination of features I wanted. Rather than compromise, I built my own -- combining fluid type testing with more basic type size and font testing in a single interface.
case.roleDetail: Sole developer and designer. A personal experiment built entirely for my own use and curiosity.

decisions.title: Combining two related problems
decisions.body: Most fluid type tools focus exclusively on the clamp calculation. This tool combines that with broader type testing -- sizes, fonts, and basic typographic properties -- so you can evaluate a type scale holistically rather than in isolation. The goal was a single place to answer the question: does this type system actually work?

decisions.title: Vuex for shared type state
decisions.body: Type settings needed to be accessible and reactive across multiple parts of the interface simultaneously. Vuex handled that shared state cleanly, keeping the UI in sync as values changed.

decisions.title: Building for your own workflow
decisions.body: There's a specific kind of clarity that comes from building a tool for yourself -- you know exactly what problem you're solving and what good looks like. No user research required. The trade-off is that the feature set reflects one person's workflow, which is fine for a personal experiment.

outcome: A working tool that I use occasionally in my own workflow. More than the tool itself, it was a valuable exercise in building something from a personal itch -- understanding the CSS clamp technique deeply enough to build a testing interface around it.

title: Usability Heuristics and Scoring
blurb: A custom set of 12 usability heuristics and a 1-5 scoring system.

case.lede: A custom set of 12 usability heuristics and a 1-5 scoring system.
context: Site audits benefit from a consistent framework -- something that turns subjective usability observations into structured, repeatable findings. Existing heuristic sets, including Nielsen/Norman's well-known 10, are solid starting points but vary in coverage and have some overlap depending on the source. Rather than adopt one wholesale, I researched several sets and synthesized my own: 12 heuristics with good coverage and minimal redundancy, paired with a 1-5 scoring system that produces actionable audit results.
case.roleDetail: Sole researcher and author. Built for my own use on client and potential client site audits.

decisions.title: Synthesizing rather than adopting
decisions.body: The goal wasn't to reinvent usability theory -- it was to find the gaps and overlaps between existing frameworks and arrive at a set that felt complete without being redundant. Reviewing multiple sources made it clear that different researchers emphasize different things, and that a synthesized set could draw the best from each.

decisions.title: Coverage and clarity as the design criteria
decisions.body: Each heuristic needed to cover distinct ground and be specific enough to produce consistent scores across different auditors and different sites. The 12 heuristics cover structure and navigation, user control, feedback, predictability, error handling, learnability, aesthetic restraint, information availability, help and support, consistency, follow-through, and accessibility.

decisions.title: A scoring system that produces actionable results
decisions.body: Scoring runs from 1 to 5, with 5 indicating no problems. The scale is designed to distinguish between failures users can't overcome, failures they can work around, functional but improvable experiences, and genuinely exceptional ones. Heuristics that don't apply to a given element are skipped rather than scored, keeping results honest.

outcome: A practical, repeatable framework for structured usability audits -- usable across client sites regardless of industry or complexity. The scoring system produces findings that are specific enough to prioritize and communicate to stakeholders.
